title: What do four ways of breaking thirty six have in common?
description: Thirty six is broken into primes in four ways, starting from two times eighteen, three times twelve, four times nine and six times six. Each way ends with two twos and two threes, and multiplying back gives thirty six every time. Keeko doubts this and says different starts must give different primes.
teaching_notes: One idea: different starting splits of a number end with the same primes, the same number of times. Watch for students who think a different first split gives a different set of primes.

source: 36 is broken in four different ways (2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6) t
video_script.why: The child sees that four different ways of breaking thirty six all end with two twos and two threes, and that multiplying back gives thirty six.
video_script.substitution: the book's own number, thirty six, broken in the book's four ways
video_script.anchor: the number thirty six broken into primes in four ways, as in the book's four breaking diagrams
video_script.wrong_answer: each way gives a different set of primes, because the first factors are different
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko sees four different first splits and says the primes at the end must be four different sets.
video_script.payoff_line: Every way ends with two twos and two threes, and they multiply back to thirty six

final_answer.spoken: two times two times three times three is thirty six in all four cases

maths_rules: every way has two 2s and two 3s
video_script.design: The four ways of breaking thirty six stand as four small trees in four colours. The primes at the bottom of each tree are counted, then multiplied back.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the number 36 with four ways of breaking it: 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9 and 6 × 6

marks.book: the title card From your book and the number 36 appear
marks.ways: four branches appear under 36, labelled 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9 and 6 × 6
marks.ask: a question mark appears under the four ways

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the number thirty six.
<bookmark mark='ways'/>It is broken in four ways. The ways start with two times eighteen, three times twelve, four times nine and six times six.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Each way is broken until only primes are left. Do the four ways end the same?

beats.on_screen: the four ways stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the first way 2 × 18 drawn as a tree: 2 is a prime and stays, 18 is not a prime and breaks into 2 × 9

marks.stop: the prime 2 is circled and stays
marks.break: 18 splits into 2 and 9 on the tree

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>A prime cannot be broken further, so it stays on the tree.
<bookmark mark='break'/>A factor that is not prime is broken again, and we go on until only primes are left.

marks.given: the four ways are written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, four ways of breaking thirty six, until only primes are left.

beats.on_screen: To find: the primes at the end of each way, and the number we get by multiplying them back
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the primes at the end of each way, and then multiply them back.

marks.first: the first tree breaks 18 into 2 × 9 and 9 into 3 × 3
marks.second: the second tree breaks 12 into 3 × 4 and 4 into 2 × 2

beats.colours: first way in teal, second way in amber
narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step one, break the first two ways. Two times eighteen breaks into two times two times nine, and then into two, two, three, three.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Three times twelve breaks into three times three times four, and then into three, three, two, two.

marks.third: the third tree breaks 4 into 2 × 2 and 9 into 3 × 3
marks.fourth: the fourth tree breaks each 6 into 2 × 3

beats.colours: third way in green, fourth way in violet
narration: <bookmark mark='third'/>Step two, break the last two ways. Four times nine breaks into two, two, three, three.
<bookmark mark='fourth'/>Six times six breaks each six into two times three, which gives two, three, two, three.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: count the primes: each of the four ways has two 2s and two 3s

marks.count: the four ways are lined up and the 2s and the 3s are circled in each

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step three, count the primes in each way. Every way has two twos and two threes, though the order changes.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check by multiplying back: 2 × 2 = 4 and 3 × 3 = 9, then 4 × 9 = 36
beats.colours: 2s in teal, 3s in amber, 36 in gold
narration: <bookmark mark='twos'/>Step four, multiply back to check. Two times two is four.
<bookmark mark='threes'/>Three times three is nine.
<bookmark mark='join'/>Four times nine is thirty six, and order does not change this.

marks.ans: the answer is boxed in green

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Every way ends with two twos and two threes, and they multiply back to thirty six. This holds in all four cases.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the board
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble says each way gives a different set of primes; the four starts 2, 3, 4, 6 are shown above the same four primes at the bottom; the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

marks.starts: the four first factors 2, 3, 4 and 6 light up in a row
marks.ends: the same four primes 2, 2, 3, 3 light up under every start

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks each way gives a different set of primes, because the first factors are different.
<bookmark mark='starts'/>The starts are two, three, four and six, and they do differ.
<bookmark mark='ends'/>But look at the bottom of the trees. The same two twos and two threes appear every time.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>Different starts need not mean different ends.
